chapters.relation: This span (the book's front matter plus the Part I 'Hook-Up Culture' essays) argues that college hook-up culture can be examined philosophically rather than merely lived. Hole and Chen recast reckless sexual 'experimentation' as a Socratic self-experiment, having students name a change, run it, and interrogate a 'big question' (e.g. Chen's dare to abstain all freshman year) to become a 'wiser lover.' Romaya argues that gay and lesbian students' opposite-sex 'straight sex experiments' undermine fixed sexual identity, invoking Buddhist anatman and Hume's bundle theory to reject a static self. Bruce gives a phenomenological reading of how Facebook/MySpace profiles and text/level-jumping alienate courting students, and Lunceford treats the 'walk of shame' outfit via Peirce's index/symbol semiotics as a sign of feminine sexuality marked shameful.

chapters.file: ch20 - College Sex - Philosophy for Everyone Philosophers With Benefits.md
chapters.relation: This span closes the walk-of-shame semiotics and then applies ancient ethics to college relationships. Puka defends long-distance college relationships through Aristotle's account of philia—arguing (provocatively, per Aristotle) that love is an activity, so being apart 'murders' love unless couples make Skype, sexting, and texting into the relationship's real medium rather than a substitute. Stephens brings Epicurus and Lucretius to 'friends with benefits': since sexual passion is a natural-but-unnecessary desire that breeds anxiety and love is a wound to the mind, while friendship is necessary for ataraxia, he concludes students should skip the sex and keep the friend—'friends are the real benefits,' echoing Tina Turner's 'What's Love Got to Do with It?' Levine/Mongeau and Smith/Morrison supply communication-research data on how FWB relationships form, are negotiated (usually not), and often end when one partner 'catches feelings.'

chapters.file: ch21 - College Sex - Philosophy for Everyone Philosophers With Benefits.md
chapters.relation: This span turns to the ethics and epistemology of college sex. Kania argues there is no clear line between close friendship and a sexual relationship, so condemning student-professor sex logically forces condemning student-professor friendship—rejecting Golash's split and defending carefully-conducted consensual relationships. Layne narrates Socrates/Alcibiades, Abelard/Heloise, and Heidegger/Arendt to contrast Socratic eros (Plato's Symposium, love as a friend of wisdom directed at the soul) and Heideggerian authentic love ('I want you to be what you are') against Abelard's exploitative lust. McDowell mines epistemology (justification, taking beliefs 'to heart,' reflective equilibrium) to argue better thinking yields better, more autonomous sex. Pinku weighs 'plain sex' against Nagel's interpersonal-arousal account of embodiment to ask whether sex needs love, and Brophy uses Kantian dignity (treating the body as a mere means, not an end) to argue that prostitution and webcam porn undertaken to pay tuition violate the student's autonomy.
